name: Steroid cell tumour of the ovary
aliases: steroid cell tumour not otherwise specified

reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: A rare sex cord-stromal tumour composed of cells resembling steroid-secreting cells, frequently producing androgens and causing virilisation
Most commonly secretes testosterone, so hirsutism, oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, and virilisation are typical presenting features
Some tumours instead secrete oestrogen or cortisol, occasionally producing a Cushingoid picture
Subclassified into stromal luteoma, Leydig cell tumour, and steroid cell tumour not otherwise specified, the last being the most common and having the greatest malignant potential
Leydig cell tumours may contain characteristic cytoplasmic Reinke crystals
Usually unilateral; larger size, mitotic activity, necrosis, and atypia point towards malignant behaviour
Managed surgically, with fertility-sparing options for benign-appearing tumours in young women and resolution of androgenic features after removal
reference.pathophysiology: Steroid cell tumours are sex cord-stromal neoplasms made up of cells with abundant eosinophilic or lipid-rich cytoplasm that resemble luteinised stromal cells, Leydig cells, or adrenocortical cells, and characteristically synthesise steroid hormones. Androgen production, most often testosterone, is the usual functional consequence and drives virilisation, although some tumours elaborate oestrogen or, less commonly, cortisol with resulting Cushingoid features. The category is divided into stromal luteoma and Leydig cell tumour, which are almost always benign, and steroid cell tumour not otherwise specified, which accounts for most cases and carries a definite risk of malignant behaviour. Malignancy is suggested by larger size, increased mitotic activity, necrosis, haemorrhage, and nuclear atypia rather than by hormonal output.
additionalInvestigations: Serum testosterone and full androgen profile to confirm hyperandrogenism
Cortisol and adrenal axis testing when a Cushingoid picture is present
Transvaginal ultrasound to identify a solid ovarian mass
Adrenal and pelvic cross-sectional imaging to localise the hormone source
Histology with assessment of size, mitoses, necrosis, and atypia to gauge malignant potential
Immunohistochemistry (e.g. inhibin, calretinin, Melan-A) to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Rapidly progressive virilisation with markedly raised testosterone and an ovarian mass
A Cushingoid presentation from cortisol secretion
Histological features (large size, mitoses, necrosis, atypia) suggesting malignancy
Evidence of metastatic spread at presentation
reference.prognosis: Stromal luteomas and Leydig cell tumours are almost always benign and cured by excision, with hormonal effects regressing afterwards; steroid cell tumours not otherwise specified are benign in most cases but a substantial minority behave malignantly, so outlook depends on histological features and stage.
pitfalls: Attributing hyperandrogenism to polycystic ovary syndrome and missing a small functioning tumour
Failing to separate an ovarian from an adrenal source of steroid excess
Assuming all steroid cell tumours are benign and overlooking malignant features
Neglecting to reassess hormone levels after surgery to confirm cure
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Distinguish localised benign-appearing disease from tumours with malignant histological features (size, necrosis, mitotic activity, atypia), since this drives the surgical approach
In a woman wishing to preserve fertility with localised, benign-appearing disease, unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy alone is generally sufficient since disease is almost always unilateral
In postmenopausal women or tumours with malignant features at any age, perform complete surgical staging: hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and peritoneal cavity staging
For metastatic or recurrent disease, pursue surgical cytoreduction where feasible, reserving systemic therapy for gross residual, unresectable, or metastatic disease
Surgery is the primary and usually only treatment needed; there is no documented adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy benefit specific to this tumour

Consider platinum-based systemic therapy for malignant, unresectable, or metastatic disease, extrapolated from its use in other malignant ovarian sex cord-stromal and germ cell tumours rather than tumour-specific evidence
No established second-line regimen exists for this tumour type; further therapy should be individualised by a gynaecologic oncology multidisciplinary team
Radiotherapy has no established role, consistent with the general lack of radiosensitivity of ovarian sex cord-stromal tumours as a class
Follow serum testosterone (and cortisol if the tumour was Cushingoid at presentation) after treatment to confirm biochemical remission, since a rise suggests recurrence
Expect gradual resolution of hirsutism, virilisation, and menstrual disturbance after removal of the hormone-secreting tissue and support the patient through this transition
Use cross-sectional imaging surveillance for local recurrence or metastasis, with more intensive follow-up for the not-otherwise-specified subtype than for stromal luteoma or Leydig cell tumour
Refer to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team for malignant histological features, postmenopausal presentation, or when systemic therapy is being considered
Refer to endocrinology when a Cushingoid picture or complex hyperandrogenism needs distinguishing from an adrenal source before or after surgery
